stories.title: AirTrunk, Iren warn data centre investors now ‘a lot more selective’
stories.summary: AirTrunk and Iren, two of the country’s most valuable data centre and artificial intelligence infrastructure operators, say investors are becoming more discerning and favouring companies with strong…
stories.content:
AirTrunk and Iren, two of the country’s most valuable data centre and artificial intelligence infrastructure operators, say investors are becoming more discerning and favouring companies with strong records amid growing concern about bulging debts and sky-high valuations.

Surging borrowing costs and fears that ambitious expansion plans can’t be delivered have already foiled plans for a $44 billion listing of Firmus Technologies, with the corporate regulator disclosing that it was “undertaking inquiries” into the failure of the float this month.

stories.summary: Forecasts slashed after community opposition stalls AI expansion plans

# Australian data center operator NextDC shares fall 40% after power backlash

Forecasts slashed after community opposition stalls AI expansion plans

NextDC has data centers in Australia, including this Sydney collaboration with OpenAI, New Zealand, Malaysia and Japan. © Getty Images

SHAUN TURTON

October 21, 2026 15:04 JST

CANBERRA -- Major Australian data center operator NextDC's shares tumbled 40% on Wednesday after the company revealed that a public backlash had stalled plans to increase power supply to a flagship site in Melbourne, underscoring the challenges facing the rollout of in-demand artificial intelligence infrastructure.

stories.title: Microsoft scraps UK data centre deal with Nscale, Telegraph says
stories.summary: The facility’s site has been contending with a series of delays, the newspaper adds

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic

stories.content:
The facility’s site has been contending with a series of delays, the newspaper adds

\[LONDON\] Microsoft has pulled out of a UK data centre deal with British neocloud Nscale at a critical time for the startup’s initial public offering hopes, the *Telegraph* reported.

The newspaper did not provide a specific reason for why the US tech giant had pulled the plug on the deal in Loughton, Essex, though it said the site has been contending with a series of delays.

Authorities have told Nscale they do not expect a power supply to the facility until the 2030s, it added.

Nscale’s flagship site in Norway is also six months behind schedule, with only 6.4 megawatts (MW) of the intended 30 MW data centre up and running.

Nscale relies on Microsoft and Anthropic for around 85 per cent of its contracts, going by an IPO filing, and the former had been set to become the anchor tenant at Nscale’s first British data centre in Essex.

Microsoft’s withdrawal would mark a setback for the company that is seeking to raise as much as US$3 billion in an IPO as soon as October, and which was already contending with investor jitters over the risks of the wider artificial intelligence build-out.

Nscale is one of the most prominent neoclouds, a new group of companies seeking to build huge computer complexes for AI.

They want to cash in on the hundreds of billions of dollars big tech companies have pledged to spend on the technology and are a key part of the AI boom’s supply chain.

An Nscale spokesperson told the *Telegraph*: “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK.

“Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts.”

Microsoft did not comment to the *Telegraph* and did not immediately respond to queries by Bloomberg.

The backdrop to Nscale’s IPO ambitions has turned gloomier in recent days, with fellow neocloud CoreWeave in the spotlight last week after the co-founder said the company was exploring ways to borrow in investment-grade debt markets, where there are vast pools of money from insurers to tap.

Investors had already grown cautious of AI computing suppliers due to the tens of billions of dollars they and their customers are borrowing to finance the massive build-out of data-centre capacity.

CoreWeave shares plunged in the first three sessions of the week, then bounced back somewhat, before concern returned on Friday, leading to the the stock’s worst week since November with a 25 per cent drop.

That also came in the wake of Australian data centre company Firmus scrapping its plans for an IPO, after the deal failed to garner enough support for the marketed share price. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: CapitaLand India Trust unveils US$203.2 million Chennai data centre
stories.summary: The 53 MW facility is due for completion by end-2026

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic

stories.content:
The 53 MW facility is due for completion by end-2026

\[SINGAPORE\] has launched a new data centre in Chennai entailing an investment of about 19.4 billion rupees (US$203.2 million), even as its sponsor and manager expands its digital infrastructure footprint in India.

CapitaLand Data Centre Chennai 01, Clint’s first data centre development in the state of Tamil Nadu, will have a gross power capacity of 53 megawatts (MW) when completed by the end of 2026.

The project was launched on Thursday (Oct 15) by Singapore Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade) Gan Kim Yong and the chief minister of Tamil Nadu, C Joseph Vijay.

Located in Ambattur, an established data centre corridor in Chennai, the development is jointly held by Clint and the CapitaLand India Data Centre Fund.

The facility will have 34 MW of power capacity for IT equipment across 13 data halls. It is designed to support high-density computing systems, including those using liquid cooling, and offer customers a choice of network providers.

The CEO of Clint’s manager, Gauri Shankar Nagabhushanam, said: “The development reflects our conviction in the long-term growth of India’s data centre sector, and is designed to meet the evolving requirements of hyperscale and enterprise customers.”

The Chennai project follows Clint’s data centre development in Navi Mumbai, which has been fully leased to a leading global hyperscaler.

CLI said it intends to continue expanding its data centre, logistics and industrial portfolio in Tamil Nadu through its listed and private fund platforms.

The group has operated in the state for 22 years, and has invested more than 60 billion rupees in seven operational assets.

Its Tamil Nadu portfolio encompasses business parks, industrial and logistics facilities, lodging and digital infrastructure. CLI first entered the state through International Tech Park Chennai in 2004.

CLI India chief executive Quaiser Parvez said the group is positioned to support Tamil Nadu’s growth as a technology, manufacturing and digital economy hub through its investment, development and fund-management capabilities.

India is a core market for CLI. Its funds under management in the country exceeded S$8 billion as at Jun 30.

Its India portfolio comprises nine business parks, 14 industrial and logistics properties, four data centres under development and three co-working spaces.

Its lodging arm, , manages about 6,300 units in 24 operating and pipeline hotels and serviced residences in India.

stories.title: Thailand fast-tracks data center rules for trillion baht investments
stories.summary: Thailand is accelerating regulatory guidelines for data center businesses. This aims to provide clarity on land use, infrastructure, and community safety standards for over 1 trillion baht in investments.
stories.content:
Thailand is accelerating the finalisation of regulatory guidelines for data center businesses, as investors await clarity on land use, infrastructure requirements, and community safety standards.The Data Center Policy Committee is scheduled to meet to address outstanding issues. A draft framework is expected to take shape in the first quarter of 2027.The Ministry of Digital Economy and Society is collaborating with the Big Data Institute to develop the TH-DC Dashboard. This dashboard will consolidate information on investment projects and infrastructure requirements.Four subcommittees are reviewing economic policy, data integration, infrastructure, land use, and urban planning. This aims to establish common regulatory standards, according to Bangkokbiznews.Nan Boonthida Somchai, Deputy Minister for Digital Economy and Society, stated that classifying data centers under industrial and urban planning regulations is a main challenge. This classification will influence where facilities can be built and the conditions they must meet, particularly regarding electricity, water, telecommunications infrastructure, and environmental safety.Proposed community safety requirements include minimum distances between data centers and residential areas, schools, hospitals, and temples. These distances are based on the volume of fuel stored on site.Facilities storing between 90,000 and 180,000 litres would need to maintain a distance of at least 100 metres. Those storing between 180,000 and 500,000 litres would require at least 200 metres. These proposals remain under review and would form part of a wider licensing assessment.The government faces pressure to finalise the framework as projects worth more than 1 trillion baht (US$30 billion) are awaiting regulatory clarity. These investment plans are held by the Board of Investment.Affected projects include operational facilities, developments under construction lacking some required approvals, particularly for electricity use, and proposed investments yet to begin construction. The new guidelines are not expected to apply retroactively to existing projects. However, operators must continue to meet existing legal requirements, including those covering fuel storage, electricity consumption, and telecommunications connections.Prolonged regulatory uncertainty could prompt investors to redirect projects to other markets. The government seeks to strengthen Thailand’s position as a regional digital infrastructure and AI hub.

stories.title: Extreme weather raises data centre downtime risk
stories.summary: Persistent severe weather conditions, including heatwaves and floods, pose a constant threat to critical infrastructure globally. Data centres face significant financial losses from downtime, ranging from $300,000 to $540,000 per hour. Proactive monitoring and resilience strategies are essential for maintaining uninterrupted operations.
stories.content:
Severe weather conditions, such as cyclones, storms, heatwaves, floods, and droughts, continuously endanger critical infrastructure worldwide.Heatwaves and droughts are the second-deadliest weather category. They cause critical infrastructure instability, power line inefficiency, and overloaded transformers. This can lead to load shedding or automatic shutdowns of critical systems.The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) reported 2023 as the fifth-warmest year in the 129-year record for the United States.Uninterrupted operations at healthcare facilities can cost over $600,000 per hour due to delayed care and lost surgical volume. Interruptions in manufacturing facilities average about $260,000 per hour.In data centres, downtime costs range between $300,000 to $540,000 per hour. These costs are driven by customer churn, data recovery efforts, and service level agreement (SLA) penalties.To maintain continuous operations, critical infrastructure organisations require solutions for proactive monitoring and alerting of mechanical and electrical systems. Continuous monitoring provides real-time equipment and system views, ensuring optimal operations regardless of external conditions.Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) and Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) platforms enable teams to monitor and analyse data from various sources over time. These platforms offer real-time alerts and actionable insights, expediting tactical equipment repairs without manual on-site inspections.Extreme heat increases electricity demand to record highs while straining all aspects of the grid. Surging temperatures affect the entire infrastructure ecosystem, from power generation to local distribution lines.The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) recorded a peak load of 91.1 gigawatts (GW) in July. The PJM Interconnection, serving 13 mid-Atlantic states, reported power demand hitting 162 GW, its second-highest level ever. Local utilities request customers to conserve electricity during peak hours to prevent blackouts.The U.S. Department of Energy has authorised emergency orders. These allow grid operators to direct large energy users, including data centres, to switch to backup generation. This occurs before severe emergency alerts are declared.Organisations must implement comprehensive monitoring systems that integrate across portfolio sites and existing devices. Preventive maintenance of legacy and new equipment helps avoid major failures and costly shutdowns.Cooling system failures can cause equipment to overheat, leading to controlled shutdowns. This impacts services at data centres, telecom towers, and utility distribution centres. Operating systems at higher loads increases energy consumption and causes premature component failure.Engineers designing systems must consider equipment limitations relative to overall system capabilities. They should use regionally updated weather data for cooling load calculations, as historical averages are unreliable. Choosing units with wider coil surface areas helps meet rising heatwave demands. Better ventilation in mechanical rooms or rooftop airflow can release trapped heat. Optimising controls with smart staging for compressors with multi-stage or variable speeds is also crucial.

- Operations & Resilience

stories.title: DayOne said to weigh options including delay, size cut for US IPO after data centre rout
stories.summary: It has not made a final decision and may still move ahead with the offering in the coming weeks

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic
The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
It has not made a final decision and may still move ahead with the offering in the coming weeks

\[HONG KONG\] DayOne Data Centers is weighing options for its US initial public offering, including a potential delay or size cut, as volatility around data centres increases, according to people familiar with the matter.

While Singapore-based DayOne has been waiting for the right window to launch the IPO, it has also been considering the possibility of pushing back the share sale until the market recovers, the people said.

Other options include going ahead with a smaller listing that may raise US$2.5 billion to US$3 billion, roughly half of what it had originally aimed for, the people said.

DayOne, whose backers include Coatue and Hillhouse, is continuing to engage with potential investors and still wants to move forward as soon as the market allows, the people said.

The company was initially considering raising as much as US$5 billion from the listing as soon as the fourth quarter, people familiar with the matter said previously. It had been eyeing a valuation of about US$20 billion, the people have said.

Deliberations are ongoing and DayOne has not made any final decisions, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private.

The company could still opt to move ahead with the offering in the coming weeks, according to the people. DayOne declined to comment.

While data centres have drawn global investor demand amid a boom in sectors related to artificial intelligence, a more negative sentiment has started to have ripple effects on IPOs.

DayOne has been raising billions of dollars in private funding rounds as it seeks capital to build out its pipeline.

Australian data centre company Firmus Grid pulled its roughly US$5 billion IPO when investors balked at the valuation it sought, while AirTrunk, which also operates data centres, delayed a planned real estate investment trust IPO in Singapore to 2027.

South Korean digital infrastructure company Elice plunged 32 per cent in its Seoul trading debut on Tuesday.

Coreweave’s shares have more than halved since their May peak, and Nscale is facing pushback over its target IPO valuation, Bloomberg News has reported.

On Wednesday, shares of Australian data centre operator Nextdc plummeted after it cut earnings guidance.

Some investors are hoping that the recent market volatility will pass after the US midterm elections on Nov 3. They are also looking ahead to the performance of Anthropic’s upcoming listing as an important gauge of sentiment towards the AI sector.

DayOne filed for a US IPO earlier in October. The offering is being led by Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase & Co, Bank of America and Citigroup.

IFR reported on Monday that DayOne was gathering more investor feedback before launching the share sale.

DayOne is running or developing data centres in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Hong Kong, Japan, Finland and Spain. Other backers include GDS Holdings, the SoftBank Vision Fund and Citadel’s Ken Griffin. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: Thailand moves to finalise data center rules amid trillion baht investment pipeline
stories.summary: Thailand is accelerating work on regulatory guidelines for data center businesses as investors await clarity on land use, infrastructure requirements and community safety standards. The Data Center Policy Committee is scheduled to meet and address outstanding issues, with a draft framework expected to take shape in the first quarter of 2027. The Ministry of Digital […]
stories.content:
Thailand is accelerating work on regulatory guidelines for data center businesses as investors await clarity on land use, infrastructure requirements and community safety standards. The Data Center Policy Committee is scheduled to meet and address outstanding issues, with a draft framework expected to take shape in the first quarter of 2027.

The Ministry of Digital Economy and Society is working with the Big Data Institute to develop the TH-DC Dashboard, which will consolidate information on investment projects and infrastructure requirements. Four subcommittees are also reviewing economic policy, data integration, infrastructure, land use and urban planning to establish common regulatory standards according to an article by Bangkokbiznews.

Nan Boonthida Somchai, Digital Economy and Society, Deputy Minister, revealed that the main challenge is determining how data centers should be classified under industrial and urban planning regulations. The classification will influence where facilities can be built and the conditions they must meet, particularly regarding electricity, water, telecommunications infrastructure and environmental safety.

Proposed community safety requirements include minimum distances between data centers and residential areas, schools, hospitals and temples, based on the volume of fuel stored on site. Facilities storing between 90,000 and 180,000 liters would need to maintain a distance of at least 100 meters, while those storing between 180,000 and 500,000 liters would require at least 200 meters. The proposals remain under review and would form part of a wider licensing assessment.

The government faces pressure to finalise the framework as projects worth more than 1 trillion baht (US$ 30 billion) are awaiting regulatory clarity, according to investment plans held by the Board of Investment. Affected projects include operational facilities, developments under construction that lack some required approvals, particularly for electricity use, and proposed investments that have yet to begin construction.

The new guidelines are not expected to apply retroactively to existing projects. However, operators must continue to meet existing legal requirements, including regulations covering fuel storage, electricity consumption and telecommunications connections.

The government is seeking to strengthen Thailand’s position as a regional digital infrastructure and AI hub, but prolonged regulatory uncertainty could prompt investors to redirect projects to other markets.

According to an ICT market analysis from Mordor Intelligence, Thailand’s ICT market is projected to grow from US$ 17.74 billion in 2025 to US$ 33.08 billion by 2031, at a 10.95 percent CAGR. Growth is driven by nationwide 5G expansion, hyperscale data-center investments, government cloud-first initiatives, Industry 4.0 modernization, rising cybersecurity demand, and fintech development.

stories.title: Prefabricated IT pods cut data center installation time by 80 per cent
stories.summary: A study by Schneider Electric and Compass Datacenters found that prefabricated, liquid-cooled IT pods reduced onsite installation time by 80 per cent. The analyzed schedule decreased from 75.5 hours to 15 hours for white-space infrastructure.
stories.content:
Schneider Electric and Compass Datacenters collaborated to quantify time savings from prefabricated liquid-cooled IT pods. Their joint study found an 80 per cent reduction in onsite installation time for white-space infrastructure. This compared to traditional methods, with the schedule decreasing from 75.5 hours to 15 hours.The study focused on preparing the pod for IT equipment installation. It used durations observed during a Compass Datacenters deployment. The traditional comparison combined observed containment-installation durations with schedules from mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) specialists.Modern high-density deployments are more complex. They often include higher-capacity power distribution, denser cable-support systems, and overhead piping for liquid cooling. Traditionally, these systems arrive separately and are installed onsite through multiple activities.Compass Datacenters deploys prefabricated IT pods, integrating key elements onto the pod frame in a manufacturing environment. For the deployment studied, Schneider Electric and Compass Datacenters co-engineered a high-density, liquid-cooled IT pod. This approach incorporates TCS piping, busway, cable-support infrastructure, and containment into the pod design.This allows selected infrastructure to be installed, aligned, inspected, and tested during manufacturing. Site preparation can also proceed in parallel. The reduction did not come from faster field activities by crews. Instead, it resulted from avoiding separate onsite installation for components like TCS piping, busway, and cable shelving.Prefabricated designs offer broader benefits beyond deployment speed. Standardised design and installation improve predictability. They also shift portions of inspection and quality verification to a controlled manufacturing environment. For example, factory-installed TCS piping sections can be cleaned, passivated, and leak-tested before shipment.

- Construction & Site Development

# Prefabricated IT pods cut data center installation time by 80 per cent

A study by Schneider Electric and Compass Datacenters found that prefabricated, liquid-cooled IT pods reduced onsite installation time by 80 per cent. The analyzed schedule decreased from 75.5 hours to 15 hours for white-space infrastructure.

stories.title: AI demand reshapes data center power, grid, and supply chains
stories.summary: Machine-generated web requests surpassed human traffic for the first time in June, according to Cloudflare data, driving a shift from north-south to east-west traffic between agents and data centers. This trend highlights increasing constraints on power, grid timelines, equipment, and skilled labour within the data center industry.
stories.content:
The data center industry is grappling with new challenges as artificial intelligence (AI) demand redefines infrastructure requirements, with machine-generated web page requests now exceeding human traffic. This shift, noted at Capacity Europe 2026, necessitates changes in network architecture and supply chain planning.Cloudflare data for June showed machine-generated web page requests at 57.4 per cent, surpassing human requests for the first time. Colt chief strategy officer Avijit Singh projected that machine traffic could increase by 100 times within five years, transforming traffic flows from cloud-to-user to inter-data centre communication. This transition demands higher latency, resilience, automation, and observability, while shifting security focus towards verifying machine identity.
### Inference and Edge Computing

The industry is increasingly focused on AI inference workloads, which are now matching training investments, according to Verizon's Jeff Hulse, citing McKinsey research. Orange Wholesale's Valerie Cussac noted that AI workloads are already impacting networks, particularly between data centres. This has revived interest in edge computing, with T Wholesale's Dimitrios Rizoulis observing high demand for edge locations in Europe. DE-CIX CEO Ivo Ivanov stated that each millisecond of latency equates to approximately 80 kilometres, positioning agentic AI applications within 100 to 150 kilometres of their inference processing. Meta, which has deployed edge sites since 2013, called the industry's earlier retreat from edge a "major missed opportunity," noting current scarcity in edge capacity.
### Connectivity and Supply Chain Bottlenecks

Connectivity planning often occurs too late in data centre builds, Digital Realty's Paula Cogan said, emphasising the need for a deep connectivity ecosystem. Colt's Joe Scattareggia mentioned that new fibre builds take 12 to 18 months, with Equinix planning connectivity five years in advance for one North London campus. Exa Infrastructure CEO Jim Fagan highlighted a "fundamental shift" in demand, with Salam's Amjad Arab stating that AI workloads can require up to 36 times more fibre than traditional applications. This demand extends beyond major hubs to local markets and enterprise sites, requiring the "whole network," euNetworks CEO Marisa Trisolino said.Long-haul and subsea capacity face significant underinvestment, according to FLAG's Paul Abfalter, leading to constraints on international routes. Sparkle CEO Enrico Bagnasco indicated that geopolitics is hindering sufficient subsea capacity development over the next five years, particularly in US and Middle East regions. Orange announced a joint venture for Pisces, a 3,125-kilometre subsea system linking Ireland, France, Spain, and Portugal.Supply chain delays are also impacting operations, with Telehouse's Ozgur Duzgunoglu reporting two-year lead times for generators and 12 to 18 months for high-voltage transformers. Greenscale's Miriam van Kooperen expressed concern about capacity, as operators commit to suppliers before design finalisation. Start Campus has adopted a "procure first, design around it" approach, with Nelson Pinto de Magalhaes measuring procurement savings in days rather than euros. Operators are also shifting to performance-based specifications to allow supplier flexibility.
### Power and Labour Constraints

Power remains a dominant constraint, with grid certainty being a larger problem than availability. An investor noted that grid operators might promise connections in 36 months but deliver in 48, burdening developers with extra capital costs. National Grid's David Atkins said the UK transmission owner is building three times more network in the current five-year period. He added that a 1 to 2 per cent flexibility from data centres could unlock significant spare capacity. Securing power in Frankfurt can take five to seven years, and anchoring a new facility in Europe takes three to four years, compared to 18 months in the US, according to Meta. This pushes operators towards behind-the-meter power solutions.Skilled labour is emerging as another critical bottleneck. Pinto de Magalhaes highlighted the difficulty of coordinating equipment, installers, and commissioning teams. Van Kooperen anticipates significant shortages in mechanical, electrical, and plumbing trades by 2029, especially in new data centre locations. Community consent is also a growing concern, with Digital Realty's Paula Cogan advocating for initiatives like Infrastructure for America to improve public understanding of data centres' local economic impact.

# AI demand reshapes data center power, grid, and supply chains

Machine-generated web requests surpassed human traffic for the first time in June, according to Cloudflare data, driving a shift from north-south to east-west traffic between agents and data centers. This trend highlights increasing constraints on power, grid timelines, equipment, and skilled labour within the data center industry.

- Published On Oct 21, 2026 at 07:40 AM IST

## Highlights

- Machine-generated web traffic surpassed human traffic in June, reaching 57.4 per cent, according to Cloudflare data.
- AI inference workloads are now matching training investments, driving demand for edge computing locations in Europe.
- Data centre equipment like generators face two-year lead times, and high-voltage transformers take 12 to 18 months.
- Power grid certainty is a major constraint, with power connections in Europe taking up to five to seven years.

stories.title: NextDC cuts FY27 guidance, pauses new projects over M3 power delay
stories.summary: Australian data centre operator NextDC has sharply reduced its FY2027 revenue and earnings guidance after delays to electricity network works at its M3 Melbourne campus, with the company also pausing new development projects and land acquisitions while it reviews capital expenditure. NextDC has cut its FY2027 net revenue guidance to AU$475 million-AU$500 million, from AU$615 […]
stories.content:
Australian data centre operator NextDC has sharply reduced its FY2027 revenue and earnings guidance after delays to electricity network works at its M3 Melbourne campus, with the company also pausing new development projects and land acquisitions while it reviews capital expenditure.

NextDC has cut its FY2027 net revenue guidance to AU$475 million-AU$500 million, from AU$615 million-AU$640 million previously. The revised guidance excludes the affected M3 customer contracts, including capacity already billing, because NextDC said it could not reliably estimate their FY2027 contribution amid uncertainty over power supply and contractual obligations.

Underlying EBITDA guidance has been reduced to AU$245 million-AU$265 million, down from AU$385 million-AU$410 million, according to an ASX announcement on 21 October.

The revisions primarily reflect delays to 66kV electricity network augmentation works by Jemena Electricity Networks, which supplies power to the M3 campus in Melbourne’s inner west. Jemena suspended parts of the works in September and has since advised NextDC that it does not expect them to recommence before February 2027.

Jemena has attributed the suspension to safety concerns and a lack of access to work sites amid community and stakeholder opposition, as well as the absence of local council consent for the works while further consultation takes place.

NextDC said the next increase in grid supply to M3 is now expected in FY2028, based on Jemena’s current indicative estimate. Delivery and billing of the contracted capacity dependent on that increase are expected to follow shortly afterwards.

The company had requested a trading halt on 19 October while it assessed the financial implications of the delay, including its FY2027 guidance.

### Customer contracts and potential service-level credits

The revised revenue and EBITDA guidance excludes revenue and attributable EBITDA from the affected M3 customer contracts, including capacity that is already billing and any potential service-level credits.

The company’s previous guidance, issued on 27 August, included approximately AU$140 million in net revenue and AU$140 million in underlying EBITDA from the affected contracts. NextDC said the exclusion of those contracts is the main reason for the revised guidance.

The company said it cannot yet reliably estimate the contracts’ contribution to FY2027 results. That will depend on discussions with the customer, the customer’s assessment of its contractual rights and obligations, whether NextDC can obtain relief under force majeure or other relevant provisions, and the accounting treatment of any service-level credits.

The contracts provide for service-level credits where capacity is delivered late or is not fully powered and, in some circumstances, give the customer rights to terminate. NextDC said it is assessing the potential implications of the delays under those contracts.

The company stressed that the capacity remains under contract, subject to the customer’s rights, and that construction of the data halls is continuing. It is working with the customer on a revised power ramp and with Jemena to bring forward power delivery.

NextDC chief executive and managing director Craig Scroggie said the company had removed the affected contracts from its FY2027 guidance until it could reliably estimate their contribution. “The timing and scale of their contribution remain uncertain,” Scroggie said.

NextDC added that service-level credits payable on the affected contracts could reduce underlying EBITDA below the revised guidance.

### Capital expenditure review and development pause

NextDC has also reduced its FY2027 capital expenditure guidance to AU$4.5 billion-AU$5 billion, from AU$5.25 billion-AU$5.75 billion previously, a reduction of AU$750 million, or 13%-14%. The previous guidance did not include capitalised interest.

The revised range includes approximately AU$500 million of reimbursable customer fit-out costs and AU$230 million of capitalised interest. Excluding capitalised interest, the company said the revised guidance represents a like-for-like reduction of approximately AU$980 million, or 17%-19%, from its previous range.

The reduction primarily reflects the deferral of expenditure on uncontracted data centre expansion projects, corporate technology and other projects.

NextDC said it had put all new development projects and land acquisitions on hold for the foreseeable future, focusing capital expenditure on contracted customer capacity expected to be delivered over the next 12–18 months and development work already close to completion.

The board has begun a detailed review of the capital expenditure programme and has committed to announcing its outcome by the company’s annual general meeting on 20 November. It will also evaluate capital-recycling opportunities, including the potential sale of development sites not required in the near term.

The company said that, with M3 revenue deferred, it had paused projects not backed by customer contracts and put that capital behind capacity its customers have already contracted.

### Liquidity and debt position

NextDC reported liquidity of AU$8.675 billion at 30 September 2026, comprising AU$1.275 billion in cash, AU$6.7 billion in undrawn senior debt facilities and a AU$700 million delayed-draw hybrid securities commitment, subject to customary conditions.

The company said it remained compliant with its financial covenants at the most recent test date of 30 June 2026 and expected to remain compliant at the next test date on 31 December.

However, NextDC noted that its ability to draw all undrawn senior debt facilities while remaining within covenant requirements would depend on the timing of drawdowns and the expected billing profiles of new customer contracts. It said a material change in expected customer billing profiles, including delays to M3 grid supply, could adversely affect its ability to draw senior debt.

The company said the earliest scheduled debt maturity is December 2029, although holders of its convertible notes may require redemption on 17 September 2029.

NextDC has not yet quantified the potential effect of the delays on the fair value of its investment properties. It expects to reflect any impact in its half-year results for the six months ending 31 December 2026.

### Further delays to M3 expansion approvals

The power supply delay is not the only timing issue affecting M3. NextDC said the Victorian government’s decision on a planning permit for M3 Stages 6 and 7 is taking longer than expected. The application, lodged in February 2026 under the government’s Development Facilitation Program, covers the planned expansion of the existing, partly operational campus.

With the Victorian government due to enter caretaker conventions from 3 November, ahead of the state election on 28 November, NextDC now expects the planning decision in 2027. Assuming the permit is granted, the later decision and delayed grid supply will affect the timing of delivery of the final stages of capacity at M3.

The company said later increases in grid supply also depend on upstream transmission projects to install new transformers at Brooklyn Terminal Station. NextDC now expects the first of these projects to be completed later than previously anticipated, affecting the timing of capacity expected to convert to billing after FY2028.

NextDC said it would continue working with Jemena and its customer to minimise the impact of the delays and provide further updates, including at its AGM on 20 November.

The community dispute has attracted wider attention. ABC News reported in September on residents’ objections to 15-metre power poles being installed in Melbourne’s inner west as part of network upgrades intended to support increased electricity demand, including that associated with data centres. Jemena said it had heard feedback that its communication and engagement could have been better, and that it had paused works to listen to community concerns.

NextDC said it already engages with the community around M3 through dedicated engagement staff and newsletters, and intends to build on this with a community engagement plan covering construction and operation of the campus, overseen by its board.

### NextDC withdraws Auckland consent application

Separately, **BusinessDesk in New Zealand** has reported that NextDC withdrew a resource consent application submitted to Auckland Council on 17 July for a proposed data centre site between Nelson and Hobson Streets in Auckland’s CBD.

The initial development was valued at approximately AU$140 million. The withdrawal has not been independently confirmed by other sources, and it is not known whether NextDC intends to submit a revised application or abandon the project.

stories.title: San Francisco shopping mall targeted for potential data center
stories.summary: Bidders competing for former Bloomingdale's site
stories.content:
A vacant mall in San Francisco, California, is being eyed for a potential data center development.

First reported by the San Francisco Chronicle, the former San Francisco City Centre Mall is being eyed for development as a data center.

KG Growth Partners has confirmed that the property was being evaluated for a project that would include a data center for an unnamed AI lab.

In June, the company asked the city about data center permitting, saying the firm is working with an unidentified potential buyer for 845 Market Street, a 350,000 sq ft (32,515 sqm) portion of the mall formerly occupied by Bloomingdale’s and owned by Macy’s. A deal for that portion of the site could reportedly be valued at around $40 million.

No application has yet been filed with the city, and it’s unclear if a deal for any part of the mall has gone through yet.

As well as a data center and offices, the project would include an AI exhibit that would be open to the public.

Earlier this month, however, San Francisco officials approved a 45-day data center moratorium in order to give the city’s planners time to research the impact of data centers on communities.

Opened in 1988, the nine-story San Francisco Centre Mall closed in January 2026 after several customers had exited the site, including Nordstrom in 2023 and Bloomingdale’s in 2025. The site totals 1.8 million sq ft (168,000 sqm) of retail and office space.

Earlier this year, Prado Group and Presidio Bay Ventures entered an agreement to buy the mall, but the deal collapsed after the pair were unable to renegotiate a long-term ground lease with the San Francisco Unified School District, which owns a portion of the land beneath the mall.

B3 Investors, a subsidiary of Austin-based B3 Commercial Management, was also reportedly looking to buy the Bloomingdale’s portion of the mall earlier this year from owner Macy’s, as well as the rest of the site.

TMG Partners and Urban Land Development have partnered and proposed converting the site into a sports and entertainment complex with basketball and volleyball courts. The San Francisco Recovery Fund is also said to be interested in the site.

stories.title: OVHcloud has 110MW of data center capacity up for grabs
stories.summary: Company reveals in its annual earnings call that it has capacity available to grow its customer base
stories.content:
OVHcloud has 250MW of data center capacity in total, according to its chairman and CEO.

Speaking during the company's annual earnings call, Octave Klaba said that of the 250MW, 140MW is operational, meaning the remaining 110MW is available. Klaba said: "That is what we will use to accelerate our growth."

Capex for OVH for fiscal year 2026 was €422 million ($474.35m), though this includes €49.5m ($55.64m) that is capex prefinanced for 2027. When considering this, capex exclusively for 2026 deployment was €372.9m ($419.16m) and 32.6 percent of revenue, up from €361.4m ($406.23m) in 2025, an incremental increase of just 3.2 percent.

Compared to other cloud providers - both hyperscale and neocloud - this is a much more conservative approach to the data center and AI buildout. Klaba noted this, calling 2026 "a year of discipline."

He said: "We managed our inventory and capex very closely while keeping operating costs under control."

Hardware costs in 2026 contributed €242m ($272m), or 21 percent of revenue, according to interim CFO Julien Rabette, which was broadly stable.

Rabette explained this as: "Two effects offset each other. First, a volume tailwind: we assembled fewer servers. Second, a price headwind: each server costing more because of component inflation. The strict capex discipline was possible thanks to our integrated model, maximizing existing assets and the front-loading of the capex."

While to date OVH has seemed more hesitant towards mass AI deployment, CEO Klaba said that in part this was because: "We didn't think that there was a lot of demand for GPUs three or four years ago. We saw competitors that invested in GPUs, and they didn't sell them in Europe, so I was a little bit cautious about the use of capex."

He added, however, that he believes the demand is now there, but that he wanted proof.

"The second is that the old GPUs, the H100s, didn’t have a lot of performance. When you have this new generation of GPUs, B300 and R200, we are talking about something different, really, a magnitude of performance more. That makes sense for the customers, and we saw that it makes sense for us, for inference, for training. Because of the reduction in cost and the \[increase in\] productivity of the capex, it’s huge. You reduce more than 20 times the cost of the same performance over just three or four years."

That said, Klaba was unwilling to provide guidance on 2027 capex, stating that it remains too variable based on customer demand, which would drive spend up, and component pricing, which could lead to a more cautious approach.

Speaking further on 2027, Klaba noted that the company has "a very good relationship with our suppliers on the RAM, hard disk, but also CPUs, GPUs, et cetera. We have continuity of the supply chain. We do not have issues delivering our growth in FY 2027." He further noted that the company has increased its prices in a "moderated way and mutualized way," and will do so again in the coming months, though declined to provide exact numbers.

Revenue for 2026 was €1.145bn ($1.29bn), up 5.6 percent Year-on-Year (YoY) from €1.08bn ($1.22bn). EBITDA was €480.5m ($539.54m), up from €437.8m ($492.11m) and up 1.6 percentage points YoY. Gross margin was 67.3 percent.

The company has also restructured its reporting segments to be split between digital starters, digital scalers, and corporates, with corporates being the largest customers. Digital starters accounted for 49 percent of revenue, scalers 31 percent, and corporates 19 percent.

Per product segment, private cloud remains OVH's largest revenue driver, bringing in €690.4m ($776.04m) for the year, or 60.3 percent of revenue.

OVH has more than 40 core data centers in operation and under construction in France, Canada, the US, Australia, Germany, Poland, Singapore, India, Italy, and the UK. These are a mix of self-built and leased locations. The company has also deployed more than a dozen Local Zone Edge locations at third-party facilities globally.

stories.title: Chief Telecom breaks ground on 16MW data center in Taiwan
stories.summary: Facility due live in 2028
stories.content:
Taiwanese data center and telecoms firm Chief Telecom has broken ground on a new facility.

Set on 1.5 hectares in the Central Taiwan Science Park (CTSP) Huwei Park, Huwei Township, Yunlin County, the facility is set to total 16MW across 3,335 sqm (35,897 sq ft). The data center is set to support both air-cooled and water-cooled cooling solutions.

The total investment for this project is approximately NT$3.3 billion (US$101m).

Official operations are expected in the second half of 2028.

In an August update, Chief said it had letters of intent (LOIs) signed by prospective clients exceeding 50 percent of the site’s available capacity.

Established in 1991, Chief Telecom is primarily a data center operator, with four data centers in Taipei, Taiwan’s capital. It is owned by Taiwan telecoms giant Chunghwa Telecom, and also operates cloud and networking services. The company runs the Taipei Internet eXchange (TPIX).

Chief launched its Liyuan 2 (LY2) facility in late 2024. The 20MW site totals 160,000 sq ft (14,865 sqm) of floor space across seven floors. The site reportedly offers 10-150kW per rack, supporting air and liquid cooling.

stories.title: Blackstone closes latest energy transition fund at $8.7bn, backs several data center focused energy firms
stories.summary: Closed 50 percent higher than the previous fund
stories.content:
US alternative asset manager Blackstone has announced the final close of its Blackstone Energy Transition Partners V at $8.7 billion, 50 percent higher than the previous interaction.

The oversubscribed fund seeks to support energy companies that deliver low-carbon energy at scale. BETP V commenced its investment period in June and has already funded three platform companies, including independent power producer Kindle Energy, Spanish energy transition firm Fisterra, and private electric transmission utility Viridon.

The fund has also acquired three companies that focus on energy efficiency and resiliency. These include Flow Control, a US provider of flow control solutions and components for data center liquid cooling, Dresser Utility Solutions, a US provider of measurement (meters), control (regulators, pressure relief valves), and infrastructure repair products for gas and water utilities, and DarkVision, a Canadian provider of technology-enabled asset inspection services.

“We believe there is a generational opportunity for experienced investors in the energy transition to provide solutions to the challenges posed by growing demand for electricity,” said David Foley, global head of Blackstone Energy Transition. “By backing exceptional management teams with flexible, patient equity capital to increase manufacturing capacity, recruit and train skilled labor, and construct new critical energy infrastructure assets, BETP is delivering those solutions and, in the process, building these companies to scale, creating jobs and generating lasting value for our investors. We are deeply grateful for the trust of our investors and look forward to deploying BETP V in investments that advance the transition to a more affordable, reliable and cleaner energy future.”

The asset manager also said that it had successfully monetized several of its mature investments undertaken by its predecessor funds. This included a deal to sell US battery storage firm Aypa Power, the sale of a majority stake in Sabre Industries, a manufacturer of highly engineered critical infrastructure for power utilities, telecom and data centers, and the completion of the initial public offering (IPO) of Legence, a mechanical contracting and engineering services firm for mission-critical data center and other markets.

Blackstone has completed several data center-focused deals over 2026. In May, the firm completed an IPO of its data center real estate investment trust. The company also announced a $5.34bn investment into US natural gas firm Williams to fund the development of five behind-the-meter projects to meet growing power demand from the data center market in North America.

However, things have not all been smooth sailing for the asset manager. In September, it was reported that Blackstone’s data center joint venture with Google was hit with delays. Known internally as Project Braid, the JV was formed in May of this year and saw Google and Blackstone planning to launch a new cloud platform offering Google's Tensor Processing Units. Blackstone said it would invest $5bn in equity capital from its funds, and the two aim to bring 500MW of capacity online in 2027, with plans to expand over time.

stories.title: Developer looks to convert hotel basement into data center in Lancashire, UK
stories.summary: 66-year-old hotel getting a facelift
stories.content:
The basement of a hotel in Lancashire could be set to be turned into a data center.

Real estate company Real Big Group has filed with Burnley Council for a change of use of the Brunlea Hotel on Keirby Walk to include a data center.

The company is looking to convert the hotel’s underground car park into a data center. Close to £12 million ($16m) is reportedly set to be invested in the project, according to local press.

Full details of the planned facility haven’t been shared, but the basement area totals around 4,000 sqm (43,055 sq ft). It is unclear if there are any data center firms currently involved in the project.

The application was submitted in July, and permission was granted this month. According to submitted documents, the facility will use a closed-loop cooling system, with cooling equipment located either in the roof enclosure or underground.

Formerly known as the Keirby Hotel, the Brunlea opened in 1960. Plans emerged in 2024 for a major redevelopment of the building by Real Big Group to relaunch the site as a 32-room luxury hotel in 2027.

The roof of the data center hosts several telecom antennas.

stories.title: Nscale shops second Anthropic deal at Monarch data center campus: Report
stories.summary: Nscale, a London-based vertically integrated AI infrastructure company,is reportedly in talks to sell Anthropic US$ 44.6 billion in compute power at its Monarch data center campus in West Virginia. This is the second deal the data center developer is negotiating with Anthropic, according to Bloomberg, who spoke with people familiar with the negotiations. The deal […]
stories.content:
Nscale, a London-based vertically integrated AI infrastructure company,is reportedly in talks to sell Anthropic US$ 44.6 billion in compute power at its Monarch data center campus in West Virginia.

This is the second deal the data center developer is negotiating with Anthropic, according to Bloomberg, who spoke with people familiar with the negotiations. The deal would back a second facility at the Monarch data center campus according to sources. It is reported that Anthropic already has agreements in place with Nscale for AI infrastructure.

As reported, the deal could be finalized in the coming days, but deliberations are said to be ongoing and details of the plan could be subject to change. Neither Nscale nor Anthropic has commented on the matter publicly.

The Monarch data center campus will have 1.35 GW of capacity in its first phase with the potential to grow to over 8 GW. The project is backed by a US$ 20 billion capital investment. Nscale is working with development partners NVIDIA and Caterpillar on the campus. Microsoft had originally been expected to lease the facility, but it walked away from the site shortly after signing a letter of intent.

A similar situation played out this week when Microsoft withdrew from Nscale’s AI data center project in Loughton, Essex. It cited concerns that electricity supply problems would delay the facility’s connection to the grid.

“We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK,” Nscale said in a statement following Microsoft’s departure.

In September, w.media reported that Nscale was preparing to launch its initial public offering. The company filed a registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission but did not disclose the number of shares or the expected price range. Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan and Morgan Stanley will serve as lead bookrunners for the offering. RBC Capital Markets, BofA Securities, Deutsche Bank Securities, Credit Agricole CIB, TD Securities, Mizuho, KeyBanc Capital Markets, Cantor, SMBC Nikko and Wolfe | Nomura Alliance will act as bookrunners.

stories.title: CBRE acquires data center services firm Onnec
stories.summary: Initial purchase price of $610 million
stories.content:
NYSE-listed CBRE Group announced this week a definitive agreement to acquire Onnec Group Limited, a provider of data center infrastructure services for technology companies across Europe and Asia Pacific.

Founded in 1986 and based in London, Onnec specializes in the design, deployment, and maintenance of network, fiber, and data center infrastructure.

The initial purchase price is £460 million (approximately $610m) in cash and is expected to close by the end of the year. The pair have agreed to a multi-year earnout of up to £300m (approximately $400m), subject to Onnec meeting certain growth targets.

CBRE said Onnec is expected to generate approximately £370m ($498m) in revenue and more than £50m ($67m) of core EBITDA in 2027. After closing, Onnec will operate as part of CBRE’s Critical Infrastructure Services line of business.

“CBRE is pursuing an explicit strategy to build a global infrastructure services business to complement our real estate services business. We’ve long believed Onnec is an excellent fit in this strategy,” said Vikram Kohli, CBRE’s COO. “The acquisition is also consistent with our ongoing effort to build resilient businesses that benefit from secular tailwinds.”

Barry Horgan, chairman of Onnec, added: “From day one, our focus has been on delivering exceptional connectivity solutions for our customers. As part of CBRE, we gain the platform and expertise to broaden our capabilities, creating even greater value for our clients, and provide new opportunities for our employees, while staying true to the customer-focused approach that has driven our success.”

J.P. Morgan Securities, LLC is acting as financial advisor and Simpson, Thacher & Bartlett LLP as legal advisor to CBRE. Goldman Sachs International is acting as financial advisor and Freshfields LLP as legal advisor to Onnec.

stories.title: Magnora Data Center acquires 2MW facility in Oslo, Norway
stories.summary: Company partners with Blix
stories.content:
Magnora Data Center has acquired a data center in Oslo, Norway.

The company announced this week that it has acquired an operating data center in Oslo from an international telecom operator.

Full details haven’t been shared, but the data center totals approximately 1,400 sqm (15,070 sq ft) with up to 2MW of IT load and may be “easily upgraded” to meet the EN 50600 Availability Class 3 / Tier III standard.

Magnora DC will own 75 percent and Blix Group 25 percent of the facility. Terms of the deal weren’t shared.

Connected to existing fiber networks, Blix will connect the site to its own fiber network, linking it with the other MDATA and Blix sites in Oslo. A district heating off-taker is being evaluated for the facility.

"This project strengthens our partnership with Blix Group and adds a new, near-term deliverable to our Oslo data center pipeline. Taking over an operating facility gives us a fast track to revenue. With up to 2MW of capacity, strong security and robust fiber connectivity, the site is well suited to serve customers who need low latency, high availability, and their data kept in Norway," said Erik Sneve, chairman of Magnora Data Center.

Magnora was initially founded in 2001 and transitioned into a dedicated renewable energy investor in 2018, since investing in a number of wind, solar, and battery projects. The firm moved into data centers last year, and took its Magnora Data Center unit public in June. The company has a facility live in Norway, and has several more in development across Norway, Estonia, Finland, and Italy.

Magnora said the acquisition is the third site in the firm’s metro strategy to form a network of connected urban facilities in Oslo and around greater Oslo.

EuroNext Oslo-listed Magnora Data Center agreed to enter into a 50:50 joint venture with Blix Group in August and acquired a commercial property around Oslo to develop it into an AI data center.

Founded in 2008, Blix provides colocation services in multiple data centers in Oslo, Stockholm, Copenhagen, London, Amsterdam and New York.

Blix Solutions' existing Blix NR5 Oslo data center is located in the same building the pair acquired in August, at Nedre Rommen 5 in eastern Oslo. Opened last year, the facility offers up to 3MW across 1,000 sqm (10,763 sq ft), hosting around 144 racks.

stories.title: DataVault plans 3MW data center in Auckland, New Zealand
stories.summary: First phase due live next year, 11 carriers signed up
stories.content:
New Zealand-based colocation provider DataVault is planning a new facility in Auckland.

The company this week announced it was developing a new 3MW data center on Auckland's North Shore.

“We've already secured the North Shore building, with fit-out commencing in 2027 and the first stage scheduled to go live in the second half of the year,” the company said on LinkedIn. “And we're not starting from scratch on connectivity. We already have 11 launch partners confirmed, with more to come!”

Full details of the planned facility weren’t shared, but the 11 partners are named as EonFibre, Devoli, EdgeIX, Verge Infrastructure, WaveSquared, Vetta Group, Mercury Energy, PureLink, Vector Fibre, Vital NZ, and Megaport.

Founded in 2004, DataVault provides colocation services from its sites in Auckland, Hamilton, and Wellington.

The new facility is part of DataVault’s wider program to deliver approximately 6MW of additional capacity across Auckland, Hamilton, and Wellington over the coming years.

At its existing Grafton site at 162 Grafton Road in Auckland, Data Hall 4 is going live in Q1 2027, backed by a “significant international anchor tenant,” followed by Data Hall 5 in Q3 2027.

The Kiwi colo firm acquired a data center in Wellington from telecoms firm Vital last year.

Auckland is New Zealand’s main data hub, with more than 30 facilities operated by local or Australian-based players. Microsoft is also present in the country.

stories.title: Data centers explore front-of-the-meter power for grid capacity
stories.summary: Data center operators are exploring front-of-the-meter power arrangements to ease grid strain and expand capacity. This approach involves contributing electricity directly to the grid rather than solely for on-site use.
stories.content:
Data center operators, particularly large hyperscalers, are exploring front-of-the-meter power, an emerging strategy to address grid constraints and growing energy demand.This approach involves developing or supporting power generation capacity that delivers electricity to the broader grid, rather than reserving it exclusively for their own campuses. This differs from behind-the-meter generation, which serves a specific facility.The primary benefit for operators is improved electricity availability for future data center development, especially in markets facing long interconnection queues and delayed energisation timelines. By adding supply to the grid, companies may enhance their access to power as they expand.Front-of-the-meter strategies could also offer political and regulatory advantages, positioning data centers as contributors to grid capacity. This can help address concerns regarding the impact of new facilities on local power systems and electricity prices.However, developing or backing generation assets is capital-intensive, operationally complex, and subject to regulatory hurdles. For many operators, behind-the-meter infrastructure or utility partnerships may remain more practical in the near term.Amazon has been linked to a potential front-of-the-meter arrangement for a large AI data center in Texas. Public statements suggest the company is still exploring its options.Most data center operators currently rely on a mix of utility partnerships, long-term power procurement, energy storage, and behind-the-meter generation. The adoption of front-of-the-meter power will depend on grid constraints, utility expansion, and hyperscalers' strategic advantage in power development.

stories.title: Aolani commits 500MW AI data center capacity in Malaysia
stories.summary: Singapore-headquartered neocloud Aolani signed a Letter of Intent for 500 megawatt (MW) of AI data center capacity in Malaysia. The firm projects a commitment of up to 580MW by 2027.
stories.content:
Singapore-headquartered neocloud Aolani announced it has signed a Letter of Intent to take up 500 megawatt (MW) of AI data center capacity in Malaysia. The company projects a commitment of up to 580MW by 2027, an increase from approximately 80MW already committed in 2026.The new capacity is targeted to come online starting in the second half of 2027 across multiple sites in Malaysia. Aolani will supply the AI infrastructure, GPU deployment, and operating requirements upon completion of the sites.These sites will house purpose-built AI data centers. They are intended to support Aolani's expansion as it meets demand from global hyperscalers and AI-native companies. The firm also aims to make AI compute accessible locally.Aolani is exploring initiatives and partnerships to provide high-performance compute capacity to Malaysian sovereign AI programmes, local enterprises, researchers, and start-ups. Nicholas Chia, Chief Executive Officer at Aolani, stated that Malaysia is a vital strategic anchor for the company.Chia added that Malaysia is a proven home market where Aolani continues to grow its footprint as a hyperlocal neocloud. He noted that Malaysia is firmly established as a global hub for AI infrastructure.Chia also said that the next stage involves using local compute to catalyse development of the local AI ecosystem and the broader economy. He affirmed Aolani's commitment to steering this effort. The company plans to use this capacity expansion to work with local partners across the ecosystem to further democratise access to compute.The Letter of Intent is non-binding and is subject to the execution of definitive agreements between the parties.

Digital Realty, the cloud and carrier-neutral data center platform, has broken ground on its first data center in Türkiye, a 22 MW facility in Ankara being built through a joint venture with local investment company Rönesans Infrastructure

As announced in September, the joint venture’s first investment is poised to support growing demand for cloud, enterprise, and connectivity infrastructure in Türkiye. Land, power, and permitting had already been secured and Digital Realty expects the facility will be complete in 2028.

“Today’s groundbreaking ceremony in Ankara, Türkiye is a reflection of the long-term commitment and investment we have for our EMEA strategy at Digital Realty,” Paula Cogan, Digital Realty Managing Director and Head of EMEA, posted on LinkedIn. “In partnership with our joint venture, Rönesans Infrastructure, it’s been a truly special ceremony to see our shared vision begin to take shape, particularly in a nation with so much potential to become an even more important hub for digital infrastructure and connectivity.”

The facility in Ankara is the first step for the joint venture, which intends to develop an additional data center in Istanbul. Together, the Ankara and Istanbul facilities are expected to form a highly connected and resilient digital infrastructure platform.

“Positioned at the crossroads of Europe, the Middle East and Asia, Türkiye is emerging as an increasingly important hub for digital transformation, cloud adoption and AI innovation. This expansion complements our growing presence across Southern Europe and the Eastern Mediterranean, strengthens connectivity across our regional platform, and provides customers with greater flexibility, resilience and reach as they scale their digital infrastructure globally,” said Cogan.

Data center capacity in Türkiye is expected to grow from 350 MW in 2025 to 570 MW by 2031, according to Mordor Intelligence. Not only is the country an interconnection bridge between Europe and Asia, but the data center market growth is also being spurred along by a US$ 46.2 billion public digital-infrastructure budget allocated in 2025 as well as growing investment from global hyperscalers and regional telecom groups.

stories.title: Aolani inks Malaysia deal for 500MW AI capacity; projects 580MW commitment by 2027
stories.summary: Singapore-headquartered neocloud Aolani yesterday announced it has signed a Letter of Intent to take up 500 megawatt (MW) of AI data center capacity in Malaysia, with projected commitment of up to 580MW by 2027. This is up from approximately 80MW already committed in 2026, the firm said in a statement. The capacity is targeted to […]
stories.content:
Singapore-headquartered neocloud Aolani yesterday announced it has signed a Letter of Intent to take up 500 megawatt (MW) of AI data center capacity in Malaysia, with projected commitment of up to 580MW by 2027. This is up from approximately 80MW already committed in 2026, the firm said in a statement.

The capacity is targeted to come online starting in 2H 2027 across multiple sites in Malaysia. Under the arrangement, Aolani will, upon completion, supply the AI infrastructure, GPU deployment, and operating requirements. The sites will house purpose-built AI data centers to support the firm’s expansion as it meets demand from global hyperscalers and AI-native companies while also making AI compute accessible locally.

Aolani is also exploring initiatives and partnerships to provide high-performance compute capacity to Malaysian sovereign AI programmes, local enterprises, researchers and start-ups.

Nicholas Chia, Chief Executive Officer at Aolani, said: “Malaysia is a vital strategic anchor for Aolani and a proven home market where we continue to grow our footprint as a hyperlocal neocloud. Malaysia is already firmly established as a global hub for AI infrastructure, but the next stage is using local compute to catalyse development of the local AI ecosystem and the broader economy. We are committed to steering this effort, using this capacity expansion to work with local partners across the ecosystem to further democratise access to compute.”

The Letter of Intent is non-binding and is subject to execution of definitive agreements between the parties.

stories.title: ACE Market-bound SKA Capital eyes another RM500m in data centre-linked jobs to swell RM313m order book
stories.summary: Data centre-related projects account for nearly half of ACE Market-bound SKA Capital Bhd's RM313.4 million outstanding order book, as the group eyes more contracts from the fast-growing sector.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 20): Data centre-related projects account for nearly half of ACE Market-bound SKA Capital Bhd's RM313.4 million outstanding order book, as the group eyes more contracts from the fast-growing sector.

Managing director Datuk Subas Kumar Ambairam said the group is also bidding for about RM500 million worth of data centre-related projects through selective tenders.

Speaking at a press conference following the company's prospectus launch on Tuesday, he said the group has a success rate of about 25% for open tenders and between 40% and 45% for selective tenders.

Subas Kumar said continued investments in electricity infrastructure and data centre development would support demand for the group's engineering services.

"Every data centre needs a substation on a very fast-track basis," he said.

He added that even if data centre development slows, SKA Capital would continue to benefit from Tenaga Nasional Bhd's (KL:TENAGA) increased capital expenditure on electricity infrastructure.

The group expects underground utilities engineering to contribute about 30% of its revenue following the IPO, with the remaining 70% coming from substation engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning (EPCC) services.

SKA Capital is also seeking direct contracts from TNB through its 70%-owned subsidiary Reltency Engineering Services Sdn Bhd, while continuing to undertake civil and structural engineering works as a subcontractor.

"If the other EPCC contractors get the job, we still have a chance of getting the civil and structural works. If Reltency gets the job, we get 100% of the EPCC contract," Subas Kumar said.

He said the machinery purchases planned under the IPO would help the group execute projects more efficiently and improve margins, particularly for data centre projects that require accelerated completion.

SKA Capital's ACE Market debut is slated for Nov 11, raising over RM100 million at 43 sen per share.

stories.title: Batam data center expansion raises demand for independent water and power supplies
stories.summary: Batam’s growing data center industry is expected to require additional water and electricity infrastructure, prompting calls for operators to develop independent supplies rather than increase pressure on resources used by local residents. The infrastructure requirements extend beyond water as BP Batam estimates that existing facilities, investment commitments and planned projects represent a combined IT capacity […]
stories.content:
Batam’s growing data center industry is expected to require additional water and electricity infrastructure, prompting calls for operators to develop independent supplies rather than increase pressure on resources used by local residents. The infrastructure requirements extend beyond water as BP Batam estimates that existing facilities, investment commitments and planned projects represent a combined IT capacity of 1.47 GW, creating additional demand for reliable electricity supply.

The proposal supports BP Batam’s plan to encourage data center companies to establish their own desalination facilities in the Nongsa Special Economic Zone and Kabil industrial area. The endorsement uses Seawater Reverse Osmosis (SWRO) technology, which converts seawater into freshwater, to meet the industry’s water demand, according to a report by antaranews.

Muhammad Iftitah Sulaiman Suryanagara, Transmigration Minister, Indonesia, said, “Investment must go hand-in-hand with responsibility. Water requirements for data centers must be properly addressed, including through SWRO. The presence of data centers is not merely about technology; it also represents an opportunity for the community to secure employment, acquire skills, and earn better incomes.”

Batam has 10 data center projects in its development pipeline, including one that is already operating. The planned desalination facilities are expected to initially contribute 750 liters of water per second over the next two to three years. A subsequent expansion could raise output to 1,000 liters per second.

The expansion could strengthen Batam’s position in the global digital economy, provided infrastructure development is matched by workforce preparation and investment certainty.

The sector has already attracted major investment. In May 2026, BP Batam facilitated a US$ 5 billion project to develop an artificial intelligence data center on a 30 hectare site in Nongsa.

stories.title: ABB orders surge past expectations as data centres fuel 40% jump
stories.summary: (Oct 20): ABB Ltd reported third-quarter orders that surpassed expectations after demand for data centre and utilities electrification components surged.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
Comparable orders in the third quarter jumped 40% to $12.1 billion, the Swiss manufacturer said Tuesday. That beat an average analyst estimates of US$11.4 billion.

Separately, the company is pushing on with acquisitions, setting up a joint venture with Mitsubishi Electric Corp for a low-voltage power distribution business in Japan. ABB will pay around US$495 million for a 51% stake in the unit.

The factory automation firm has been profiting from rising investments in data centres needed to feed a surge in artificial intelligence applications. ABB makes the transformers that enable power grids to supply the centres’ substantial energy needs.

Orders in that unit were the third quarter’s key growth engine, accounting for 70% of new business. The motion business grew by 14% while automation was stable.

ABB also made a small upward tweak to its revenue forecast and now sees comparable revenue growth in the ”low teens” range. Previously it said revenue might rise in the low double-digit to low teens range.

Year to date, shares have gained around 26% through to Monday’s close. Still, given its exposure to the artificial intelligence industry and build-out, ABB has been caught in the recent faltering global AI trade that’s weighed on markets. Since the start of the month, the stock has declined 7%.

Earlier this year ABB bought British industrial components company Rotork Plc for an enterprise value of around US$5.5 billion to expand its electrification and automation businesses, its biggest ever acquisition.

ABB chief executive officer Morten Wierod has streamlined its portfolio since taking over nearly two years ago to tap into burgeoning investment in the data centres underpinning the AI boom. The Zurich-based manufacturer last year sold its robotics division for more than US$5 billion and focused on targeted acquisitions.

stories.title: This empty lot near London goes to the heart of data centre jitters
stories.summary: On London’s eastern fringe in Essex, data centre operator Nscale plans to build its £2 billion ($3.8 billion) flagship UK facility across the road from where the Bank of England produces bank notes.
stories.content:
On London’s eastern fringe in Essex, data centre operator Nscale plans to build its £2 billion ($3.8 billion) flagship UK facility across the road from where the Bank of England produces bank notes.

It’s a symbolic site. The heady rush for artificial intelligence had created a sense that data centres were a licence to print money for the likes of its owner, Josh Payne, a former Hunter Valley coal miner.
